821.quote_or_event: “Avoiding the friendship of those who resemble elephants, seek the friendship of those who resemble dogs; for an elephant will kill his driver whom he has known for a long time, but a dog will wag his tail while the spear thrown at him is still in his body.”
821.explanation: The Jain didactic anthology warns that some companions, like a war elephant, stay docile for years and then turn on the very person who has handled them longest.
821.tie_back: Valluvar's anvil, which seems to hold you up until the moment comes to strike, is the same danger as the Nālaṭiyār's elephant that kills the driver it has long known.
821.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 22 ('The choice of friends'), st. 3 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
821._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; this is a Tamil Jain text rather than canonical scripture, used because it closely matches the Kural's image of a long-trusted companion who turns and strikes when the time is right.

822.quote_or_event: “Men will remain until they have done their work in an old house the thatch of which is untied, keeping out the water by a dam, and being drenched with the rain falling down upon them. Thus will friends remain with one until their business is finished.”
822.explanation: The chapter on improper friendship in the Nālaṭiyār describes friends who stay only as long as they have something to gain, like workmen who put up with a leaking house until their job is done.
822.tie_back: Valluvar says friendship with those who only seem to be one's own shifts with what they can get; the Nālaṭiyār's friends who stay only 'until their business is finished' are the same gain-driven bond.
822.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 24 ('Improper Friendship'), st. 1 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
822._accuracy_note: Verified on wisdomlib.org (the online text has scanning typos, 'br a dam' and 'friends!', silently corrected to 'by a dam' and 'friends'; the vocative address to the 'lord of the fair and well-watered mountains' is omitted from the start). A Tamil Jain text in a chapter with the same title as this Kural chapter; it keeps the theme of gain-driven friendship but not the Kural's comparison with the courtesan's mind.

823.quote_or_event: “Though they wash it with milk and put it to dry many days, charcoal has not the property of becoming white. Though they strike with a stick, and thrust too, understanding will not enter into the body void of virtue.”
823.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār says that someone whose nature lacks goodness is not changed by instruction, just as charcoal stays black however often it is washed in milk.
823.tie_back: Valluvar warns that a hostile person who has studied many good books still does not become good at heart; the Nālaṭiyār's charcoal that milk cannot whiten makes the same point, that learning poured over a bad nature does not change it.
823.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 26 ('The want of understanding'), st. 8 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
823._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org, where stanza 8 is run into the end of stanza 7. A Tamil Jain text; it fits the claim that knowledge does not reform an unworthy heart, though it is about the unvirtuous in general rather than enemies posing as friends.

824.quote_or_event: “Anger destroys love, pride destroys modesty, deceit destroys friendship; greed is destructive of everything.”
824.explanation: Jain teaching names deceit (māyā) as one of the four passions (kaṣāya) that bind karma, and says that deceit in particular destroys friendship.
824.tie_back: Valluvar tells us to fear those who smile with the face while bitter within; the Jain verse explains why: such deceit is exactly the passion that destroys friendship.
824.source: Saman Suttam, v. 135 (from the Daśavaikālika Sūtra 8.38), English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit, via jainworld.com
824._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on jainworld.com's Saman Suttam (Samyamasutra, v. 135); canonical scripture via an anthology. It explains why deceit ruins friendship but lacks the Kural's face-versus-heart image and its advice to be wary.

825.quote_or_event: “Our intimacy with those to whom we are not bound by the chain of friendship, O king of the hills, the sides of which are covered with groves of tall sandal-trees! though it seem day by day to increase, will be dissolved as instantaneously as fire catches straw.”
825.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār warns that closeness with people who are not truly bound to us can look as if it is growing, yet it vanishes in an instant.
825.tie_back: Valluvar says nothing at all should be trusted from those not one with us in heart; the Nālaṭiyār agrees that a bond without a real 'chain of friendship' cannot be relied on, however warm it seems.
825.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 24 ('Improper Friendship'), st. 4 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
825._accuracy_note: Verified on wisdomlib.org (the online text's typo 'f'riendship' is corrected). A Tamil Jain text; it shares the Kural's distrust of friendship not rooted in the heart, but speaks of the bond's fragility rather than specifically of not trusting such people's words.

826.quote_or_event: “To join oneself to many, and strive many days and examine dispositions, and take (for friends) those who are worthy, is proper. Even with a deadly serpent, to associate and afterwards to part from it will be painful.”
826.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār advises testing people's natures over many days before taking them as friends, because it is painful to part even from a bad companion once a bond has formed.
826.tie_back: Valluvar is confident that a foe's friendly words are soon seen through; the Nālaṭiyār sets out the practical discipline behind this, a long examination of character before any friendship is accepted.
826.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 22 ('The choice of friends'), st. 10 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
826._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org. A Tamil Jain text and a next-best match: it is about testing friends' dispositions over time, not about how quickly a foe's fine words reveal themselves.

827.quote_or_event: “The absence of benevolence of disposition in him whose form is beautiful is like water mixed with milk, that is pleasant to drink. For those who are wise, to become companions of the wicked is like the nâgâ playing with the female cobra.”
827.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār's chapter on improper friendship says a pleasing exterior can hide a lack of goodwill, and that the wise who keep company with the wicked are like a snake playing with a deadly cobra.
827.tie_back: Valluvar says a foe's humble, bowing speech is like the bend of a bow, which signals harm; the Nālaṭiyār similarly warns that a pleasant surface and playful closeness can hide venom.
827.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 24 ('Improper Friendship'), st. 10 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
827._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org (diacritic in 'nâgâ' as printed). A Tamil Jain text and only a next-best match: it shares the idea of pleasant appearances hiding danger, but has nothing like the Kural's bow image or its focus on deferential speech, and the first sentence of the old translation is somewhat obscure.

828.quote_or_event: “A little monkey breaking into a fruit with its finger, will strike and seize its own father, though coming to meet it. Lord of the hills! the friendship of those who are without unity (of mind) is not pleasant.”
828.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār uses the image of a young monkey that strikes even its own father as he comes toward it, to show that closeness without unity of mind is dangerous.
828.tie_back: Valluvar says a weapon may hide in the very hands a foe joins in worship; the Nālaṭiyār's monkey that strikes the one approaching it likewise shows harm arriving through a gesture of closeness.
828.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 24 ('Improper Friendship'), st. 7 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
828._accuracy_note: Verified on wisdomlib.org (the online text's typo 'thongh' is corrected to 'though'). A Tamil Jain text and a next-best match: it shares the theme of friendship without unity of mind turning violent, but not the Kural's specific images of worshipping hands and false tears. A Jain story about a royal assassin disguised as a monk could not be verified this session and was not used.

829.quote_or_event: “It is better to be without the love of those who are without sincerity. Death is preferable to an incurable disease. To kill him at once is more desirable than to vex a man so that he becomes sore at heart, and to abuse is better than to praise one for that which we do not possess.”
829.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār says that affection from insincere people is worth less than having no affection at all, and that false praise is worse than open abuse.
829.tie_back: Valluvar advises letting a pretender's friendship die inwardly while keeping him smiling; the Nālaṭiyār agrees that insincere love is better done without, though it does not recommend answering pretence with pretence.
829.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 22 ('The choice of friends'), st. 9 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
829._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org. A Tamil Jain text giving a partial parallel only: Jain ethics, which makes straightforwardness (ārjava) the remedy for deceit, does not endorse the Kural's tactic of outward show over inner withdrawal.

830.quote_or_event: “Benevolence (maitrī) towards all living-beings (sattva), joy (pramoda) at the sight of the virtuous (guṇādhika), compassion and sympathy (kāruṇya) for the afflicted (kliśyamāna), and tolerance (mādhyasthya) towards the insolent and ill-behaved (avineya) are the other observances.”
830.explanation: The Tattvārtha Sūtra prescribes four attitudes to support the vows; toward the ill-disposed the Jain response is mādhyasthya, a detached equanimity free from both attachment and aversion.
830.tie_back: Valluvar advises being friendly in face but withholding friendship in the heart when a foe must be treated as a friend; the Jain answer is also inner detachment from the hostile, but grounded in goodwill to all beings rather than political calculation.
830.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.11 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018, via wisdomlib.org)
830._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org. Canonical for both sects; the inner detachment toward the ill-behaved partly matches the Kural's withdrawal of inner friendship, but Jain maitrī toward all beings rules out the strategic pretence the Kural allows, so the fit is partial.
